title: Submillimeter and infrared view of the Galactic Center
caption: The center of the Milky Way in submillimeter and infrared light, imaged by the APEX telescope and 2MASS
celestial: Milky Way Galactic Center · constellation Sagittarius

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This color composite looks toward the heart of our Milky Way, about 26 000 light-years from Earth. It combines two very different kinds of light to show both the stars and the giant clouds of gas and dust around them.

The gas and dust clouds come from the LABOCA instrument on the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment, or APEX, which observes at submillimeter wavelengths, around 870 micrometers. Cold dust that is dark in ordinary light glows at these long wavelengths, so APEX can map clouds that would otherwise stay hidden.

The starlight comes from the 2MASS project, which surveyed the sky in three near-infrared bands. Near-infrared light slips through much of the dust that blocks our view of the galactic center in visible light. Putting both together shows how the stars and the raw material between them are arranged. The region covered is roughly 100 light-years wide.

understand.summary: This composite combines submillimeter data from LABOCA on APEX, shown in blue, with near-infrared data from 2MASS at K-band in red, H-band in green and J-band in blue.
understand.eye: Both submillimeter and infrared light are invisible to the eye, and dust hides this region almost completely in visible light.
